newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish funds prefer Superfos Phoenix bid.
newsitem.headline: Danish funds prefer Superfos Phoenix bid.

text.p: Danish institutional investors prefer construction group Superfos' offer for roadbuilder Phoenix Contractors of the three bids currently on the table, a fund manager said on Friday.
"I absolutely favour a Superfos solution. Superfos will be able to get the most out of it," Ali Nielsen of pension fund PKA told Reuters.
In addition to Superfos, Danish builder Marius Pedersen and Norway's Rieber and Son have made offers in what is, for Denmark, unprecedented public bidding.
An analyst, who asked not to be identified, said that Superfos was also the favoured bidder of other major funds, particularly ATP.
"ATP, Denmark's biggest pension fund has its fingers in all three Danish companies involved ... with an eye to strategic considerations," he told Reuters.

ATP has a 10.4 percent stake in Phoenix, 12.67 percent in Superfos and 16.54 percent in Marius Pedersen. Danish shareholders are reluctant to see control of Phoenix pass to their Norwegian cousins, while Pedersen, with own capital of around 300 million crowns would have to borrow extensively .

Its offer, the highest of the three so far, totals 776 million crowns. To meet the bill for Phoenix it would either have to go to the loan market or issue more shares, solutions unlikely to be welcomed by the funds.
"Objectively Pedersen is simply too small...a Superfos takeover would be the best thing for investors," the analyst said.

Phoenix itself agrees that the Superfos offer, lower than Pedersen's at 767 million crowns but still considered generous by analysts, is the best for its shareholders but wants to consider broader implications.
"We want to see what benefits shareholders, workers, the local community and Phoenix's own development," vice-chairman Ivan Hermansen told Reuters after the Superfos bid on Thursday.
The Superfos offer is open until March 3 and the Phoenix board is to discuss it formally at its February 4 meeting.
The nature of the bidding has surprised Copenhagen's conservative business community where such deals are usually agreed quietly between the parties involved.
Copenhagen Stock Exchange rules demand disclosure when a buyer's stake in a company rises by five percent or to over one-third or two-thirds of the total equity.
But in practice takeovers in the past were implemented in one move, with the neccessary disclosure of the rise in a stake made together with the announcement of the acquisition.
The Copenhagen financial community is not calling the Phoenix offers hostile bids.
"We are calling it a friendly takeover to the advantage of the shareholders," PKA's Nielsen said.
Dealers are delighted at the extra share activity generated by the public takeover attempts.
On Friday mid-afternoon the Phoenix C-share was trading at 630 crowns, nearly seven percent up from its 590 crown close on Wednesday, before the Superfos and Pedersen bids.
Others are less impressed by the rough and tumble of open bidding but think its spread is now inevitable.

"I think we will see more of these kinds of offers for companies. The problem is that now that one has started the process I think that in the future you will see a lot of these things here," Nielsen said.
